## European Options

**European options** are the simplest kind of financial derivatives after
forwards and futures. Options have become a standard tool in modern finance,
allowing investors to construct contracts to hedge portfolio risk, take
advantage of perceived arbitrage and leverage risk.

:::{.definition data-title="European Option"}

A **European call/put option** is a contract giving its holder the right but
not the obligation to purchase/sell an underlying asset for some specified
strike price $K$ at some future maturity time $T$.

:::

For an underlying asset with price $S$, the payoff $h$ of a call and a put
with strike $K$ at maturity $T$ is

$$
h_{\text{call}}(S_T) = (S_T - K)^+,
\qquad
h_{\text{put}}(S_T) = (K - S_T)^+.
$$

Throughout, $C(S_t,t)$ and $P(S_t,t)$ denote the call and put prices at time
$t \le T$, and $r$ is a constant risk-free interest rate. See [[derivatives]]
for payoff diagrams.

## Pricing European Options

### Risk-Neutral Approach

By [[risk-neutral-pricing|risk-neutral pricing]], the price of a European
option at time $t$ is the expected payoff under the risk-neutral measure
$\mathbb{Q}$, adjusted for the time value of money

$$
V(t) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}\left[ D_{t,T}\, h(S_T) \mid \mathcal{F}_t \right],
$$

where $D_{t,T}$ is the discount factor from $T$ to $t$. For a constant rate,
$D_{t,T} = e^{-r(T-t)}$.

### Black-Scholes Formulas

Let $N$ denote the cumulative distribution function of the standard normal
distribution,

$$
N(x) = \mathbb{P}(Z \le x) = \int_{-\infty}^{x} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\,e^{-u^2/2}\,du,
\qquad Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1).
$$

It satisfies $N(x) + N(-x) = 1$.

:::{.theorem data-title="European Call and Put Prices"}

Under the [[black-scholes-merton-model]] the prices of a European vanilla call
and put option at time $t$ with underlying stock $S_t$, strike $K$ and
maturity $T$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}
C(S_t,t) & = N(d_{+})\,S_t - N(d_{-})\,Ke^{-r(T-t)}, \\
P(S_t,t) & = N(-d_{-})\,Ke^{-r(T-t)} - N(-d_{+})\,S_t,
\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
d_{+} = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{T-t}}
\left( \log\frac{S_t}{K} + \left( r + \frac{\sigma^2}{2} \right)(T-t) \right),
\qquad
d_{-} = d_{+} - \sigma\sqrt{T-t}.
$$

:::

These follow by evaluating the risk-neutral expectation above, using that
$S_T$ is log-normal under $\mathbb{Q}$. They also solve the
[[black-scholes-merton-model|Black-Scholes PDE]]. The sensitivities of these prices are the
[[option-greeks]].

## Put-Call Parity

:::{.theorem data-title="Put-Call Parity"}

For European options on a non-dividend-paying asset with the same strike $K$
and maturity $T$,

$$
C(S_t,t) - P(S_t,t) = S_t - Ke^{-r(T-t)}.
$$

:::

This relation does not depend on the model for $S$. It follows from the
payoff identity

$$
(S_T - K)^+ - (K - S_T)^+ = S_T - K,
$$

since taking the discounted expectation under $\mathbb{Q}$ and using that the
discounted stock price $e^{-rt}S_t$ is a $\mathbb{Q}$-martingale gives

$$
C(S_t,t) - P(S_t,t)
= e^{-r(T-t)}\,\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}[S_T - K \mid \mathcal{F}_t]
= S_t - Ke^{-r(T-t)}.
$$

The same relation comes from replication. A long call and short put
replicate a forward contract with delivery price $K$, which is worth
$S_t - Ke^{-r(T-t)}$ (buy the asset and borrow $Ke^{-r(T-t)}$). Any other
price would allow an arbitrage.

As a check, the Black-Scholes formulas satisfy parity because
$N(x) + N(-x) = 1$,

$$
C - P = S_t\left[N(d_+) + N(-d_+)\right]
- Ke^{-r(T-t)}\left[N(d_-) + N(-d_-)\right]
= S_t - Ke^{-r(T-t)}.
$$

If the asset pays dividends, $S_t$ is replaced by $S_t$ minus the present
value of the dividends. See [[black-scholes-model-with-dividends]]. Parity
also follows from the [[carr-madan-formula]].

## No-Arbitrage Bounds

Since option prices are non-negative, parity gives bounds that hold in any
model

$$
\max\left(S_t - Ke^{-r(T-t)},\, 0\right) \le C(S_t,t) \le S_t,
$$

$$
\max\left(Ke^{-r(T-t)} - S_t,\, 0\right) \le P(S_t,t) \le Ke^{-r(T-t)}.
$$

The upper bounds hold because the payoffs satisfy $(S_T-K)^+ \le S_T$ and
$(K-S_T)^+ \le K$.
